summary.short: Would give AI developers conditional immunity from state-law civil liability for errors by their AI products when used by learned professionals in professional services, if they publicly release model cards and model specifications and document limitations. Applies to acts or omissions on or after 1 December 2025.
summary.long: The bill, the Responsible Innovation and Safe Expertise Act of 2025 (RISE Act of 2025), defines developers, learned professionals, clients, errors, model cards and model specifications for AI products. Section 4 makes a developer immune from civil liability for errors generated by an AI product when used by a learned professional in providing professional services to a client, if the developer publicly releases and continuously maintains a model card and a model specification before deployment and provides documentation of known limitations, failure modes and appropriate domains of use. Model specifications may be redacted only for trade-secret information unrelated to safety, with a written justification for each redaction. Immunity is conferred only for acts or omissions that do not constitute recklessness or willful misconduct. Immunity does not apply to a developer that fails to update the model card, model specification and documentation within 30 days of deploying a new version or discovering a new and material failure mode, where that failure proximately causes a later harm. Section 4(d) applies the section to State-law claims against developers for errors arising from professional use, but not to claims based on fraud, knowing misrepresentation, or conduct outside professional use. Section 5 preserves other immunities. The Act takes effect on 1 December 2025 and applies to acts or omissions on or after that date.

relations.target_text: State-law claims against a developer for errors arising from professional use of an artificial intelligence product, where the developer is immune under Sec. 4(a)
relations.note: Sec. 4(d)(1) states express preemption of covered State-law claims. Sec. 4(d)(2) excludes State-law claims based on fraud, knowing misrepresentation, or conduct outside the scope of professional use.

evidence.quote: This section shall apply to any claim arising under State law against a developer for an error arising from the use of an artificial intelligence product

notes: Bill as introduced. No legal_basis, implements, amends, repeals or transposes relations are stated. The Sec. 3(1) cross-reference is definitional only. Internal points: the Sec. 4(d)(1) preemption applies only where immunity under Sec. 4(a) is available; Sec. 4(c) update duties run from deployment or discovery dates, while Sec. 6 applies the Act to acts or omissions on or after 1 December 2025. Sec. 3(6) sets the model-card standard by comparison to industry peers without a further measure. thresholds.note: No numeric cutoff changes legal treatment in this bill. The only numeric time limit is the 30-day update period in Sec. 4(c)(1), which is a procedural deadline (coded as an event, not a threshold). The effective date in Sec. 6 is also an event. No monetary, size, user-count or volume cutoffs appear.
